blocks.text: Another whole family of sorts works on a different instinct. Instead of comparing everything in clever sweeps, they repeatedly select one element and lock it into its final place.
Find the smallest and put it first. Or pick a pivot and drop it exactly where it belongs. Each step nails down one position for good. That is selection based sorting.
The common thread: every step chooses an element, places it in its final sorted position, and never moves it again.
The purest example is Selection Sort, and the algorithm is exactly what the name says.

items: Find the smallest element in the array.
Swap it into the first position.
Repeat for the rest of the array, ignoring the part already placed.

blocks.text: It is simple and uses no extra memory, but it always does about n^2 comparisons even if the array is already sorted. That makes it O(n^2) and too slow for large inputs.
Selection Sort is the mental model for the whole family: select the right element, place it, repeat. The smarter sorts simply select more cleverly.
Quick Sort takes the selection idea and makes it fast. Instead of hunting for the smallest each time, it picks a pivot and partitions the array so that:

items: everything smaller than the pivot ends up on its left
everything larger ends up on its right

blocks.text: After one partition, the pivot is sitting in its final sorted position. You selected its correct spot in a single pass. Then you repeat the same trick on the left and right sides.
On average this is O(n log n) and very fast in practice. Its worst case is O(n^2) when pivots are chosen badly, which good implementations avoid by picking pivots smartly.
Quick Sort is usually the fastest comparison sort in practice, which is why so many libraries use a tuned version of it under the hood.
Here is the clever part. If a partition places a pivot in its final position, then sometimes you do not need to sort the whole array at all.

Say you only want the kth smallest element. After a partition you know exactly where the pivot landed. If that is position k, you are done. If not, you only recurse into the one side that still contains k.
Throwing away half the work each time gives O(n) average time to find the kth element, far faster than fully sorting just to read one position.
QuickSelect is the secret weapon for "find the kth largest" and "top k" style questions. It finds the answer without sorting everything.

content.title: 4. Heap Sort: Selecting the Max Every Time

blocks.text: A heap is a structure that always hands you the smallest or largest element instantly. Heap Sort uses that to select elements in order.

items: Build a heap from the array.
Pop the smallest element and place it next.
Repeat until the heap is empty.

codes.python:
import heapq

def heap_sort(arr):
    heapq.heapify(arr)        # build a min heap in O(n)
    return [heapq.heappop(arr) for _ in range(len(arr))]

blocks.text: Building the heap is O(n) and each of the n pops costs O(log n), giving O(n log n) overall. It uses almost no extra memory, but it is not stable.
Each selection based sort makes a different trade. Here is the summary:

blocks.content: {"headers":["Algorithm","Average","Worst","Stable","Extra Space"],"rows":[["Selection Sort","O(n^2)","O(n^2)","No","O(1)"],["Quick Sort","O(n log n)","O(n^2)","No","O(log n)"],["Heap Sort","O(n log n)","O(n log n)","No","O(1)"],["QuickSelect","O(n)","O(n^2)","No","O(1)"]]}

blocks.text: Notice that none of them are stable. Selection based sorts move elements far across the array, which tends to scramble the order of equal items.
Pick the tool that matches the job:

items: Quick Sort: a fast general purpose sort, great as a default when stability does not matter.
QuickSelect: when you need the kth smallest or largest without fully sorting.
Heap Sort: when you want O(n log n) with almost no extra memory, or a running top k from a stream.

blocks.text: See the words "kth largest", "top k", or "k most frequent"? That is your signal to think QuickSelect or a heap, not a full sort.
